newsitem.title: USA: Three more Viper Militiamen jailed in Arizona.
newsitem.headline: Three more Viper Militiamen jailed in Arizona.

text.p: A decorated Vietnam War veteran who was an alleged leader of the self-styled Viper Militia was jailed for nine years Thursday on federal conspiracy and weapons charges.

Gary Bauer, described by prosecutors as a "technical adviser" on weapons and explosives, had pleaded guilty to 11 counts, including conspiracy to manufacture and possess explosive devices and unlawful possession of machine guns.
Two of his alleged lieutenants, Finis Walker and Randy Nelson, were given 70-month sentences and fined Thursday.
Prosecutors said it took two days to search Bauer's home after he was arrested last July and it contained so many weapons and dangerous chemicals, it was "like an ammo dump."
Assistant U.S. Attorney Fred Battista characterised Bauer as "a significant threat to the community." But Bauer's lawyer James Logan said his client was only "a foot soldier."
"He was not a decision-maker, not a leader, not an organiser ... he was a participant and little more," he said.

Bauer, who won the Bronze Star during his military service in Vietnam and showed certificates of appreciation from ex-President Richard Nixon and the commander of U.S. forces in Vietnam, Gen. William Westmoreland, was sentenced to nine years in prison, fined $16,100 and given 36 months probation.
Passing sentence, Judge Earl Carroll said of Bauer, 51: "He enjoyed what he was doing, he liked what he was doing, and he did it."
Thursday's prison terms were the harshest handed out to the nine Viper Militia members so far sentenced. On Wednesday, Carroll sentenced six members to terms up to 57 months.

A total of 12 members of the paramilitary group were arrested in a series of raids in Arizona last July by anti-terrorist agents. One more will be sentenced next week while two more militiamen have pleaded not guilty and their trial is set to start March 25.
At the time of their arrest, President Clinton said "a terrible terrorist attack" had been averted, but prosecutors later said there was no indication the suspects were planning any specific attacks.
Defence lawyers characterised the suspects as gun enthusiasts who went to remote desert areas of Arizona to "blow up dirt."

Nelson, 33, who was also fined $2,900 and put on three years probation after pleading guilty to four counts, said the militia had started out as a rifle club that "kind of got out of hand, way out of hand."

Walker, 42, pleaded guilty to three counts and was also fined $250 and put on three years probation in addition to getting a 70-month jail term. Prosecutors said he had been a recruiter for the militia.
